9335:
CAS.Verified.Expr.ValidAt.{u_1} {ι : Type u_1} (ρ : ι → ℝ) : CAS.Verified.Expr ι → Prop

Side conditions needed to justify the classical analytic derivative rules.

Rational literals carry a natural-number denominator in the AST, so validity rules out den = 0 there just as it rules out zero denominators for expression-level division.

For log, validity excludes zero, matching Mathlib's derivative theorem for the total real logarithm on both connected components of ℝ \ {0}. For sqrt, validity requires a strictly positive argument. This is stronger than what Mathlib's Real.hasDerivAt_sqrt needs (x ≠ 0, since Real.sqrt is constant on (-∞, 0]): it certifies the classical square-root branch rather than the totalized function, so a goal that is Lean-true only because of the extension to negative arguments is rejected by the reflective route. Lean's total Real.log/Real.sqrt have values outside those analytic domains, but these symbolic derivative rules certify classical differentiability. Raw Expr.eval itself is total and does not require ValidAt.

For rpow a b, validity requires a strictly positive base 0 < a, the hypothesis of Mathlib's HasFDerivAt.rpow; Lean's total Real.rpow has values for nonpositive bases that the classical power rule does not certify.

For asin and acos, validity excludes the two endpoints -1 and 1, matching Mathlib's derivative theorems for the total real inverse trigonometric functions. Arguments outside [-1, 1] are allowed: there the functions are locally constant and their derivatives are zero. Unlike sqrt and rpow, these cases do not restrict evaluation to the classical branch.

A function is continuously differentiable up to n on s if, for any point x in s, it admits continuous derivatives up to order n on a neighborhood of x in s. The parameter n belongs to ℕ∞ω (accessible in the ContDiff scope), i.e. it can be a natural number, ∞, or ω.

For n = ∞, we only require that this holds up to any finite order (where the neighborhood may depend on the finite order we consider). For n = ω, we require the function to be analytic within s at every point of s. 9082:
#cas [enclose x in [a, b], y in [c, d]] e computes an interval with rational endpoints that contains every value of e on the box of the bindings, proves it, and derives an upper bound, an absolute bound and a center with a radius.

Theorem

For the printed interval [lo, hi] the first checked step proves ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc a b, lo ≤ e ∧ e ≤ hi about Mathlib's real functions, with one ∀ y ∈ Set.Icc c d for each further binding, such as ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc 0 1, -1 / 4 ≤ x ^ 2 - x ∧ x ^ 2 - x ≤ 0 for #cas [enclose x in [0, 1]] (x ^ 2 - x). The next steps prove e ≤ u for the upper bound, |e| ≤ m for the absolute bound and |e - c| ≤ r for the center c and the radius r, which also covers the rounding of the center; decimal endpoints are rounded outward. The lemmas mem_of_enclosedOn_box, le_of_boundOn_box, abs_le_of_boundOn_abs_box and abs_sub_le_of_approxOn_box of CAS.Tactic.BoxInequality transport these statements from the checked certificate CAS.Certificate.EnclosedOn f box lo hi of the reflected form f of e (CAS.Continuum.RationalInterval.EnclosureAttempt.enclosedOn_of_interval_eq), as the tactic cega does. Each of these steps is shown when its proof succeeds within its own budget of maxHeartbeats heartbeats; otherwise the report keeps only the certificate of that view about f. Without bindings, #cas [enclose] e encloses a closed expression e.

Conditions and limits

Each binding x in [a, b] has rational literal endpoints with a ≤ b, such as -1, 3/2 or 0.1, and a box has at most 8 coordinates (cega.maxDimension). e uses the calculator grammar of #cas [N d] and |x|, and every subexpression must be defined on the whole box, so denominators exclude zero and the arguments of log stay positive. The enclosure is valid but not always tight. The Output line prints an endpoint exactly when its rational has at most 24 characters and otherwise rounds it outward to 6 decimal places; the details print the exact rationals. A center rounded this way is rounded down, and the printed radius is widened by that rounding.

Options

  • (prec := n) sets n Taylor terms for exp, n series terms for log and n binary digits for square roots; (expOrder := n), (logTerms := n) and (sqrtDigits := n) set them one at a time, with defaults 8, 10 and 12.
  • (depth := n) first refines the box by checked bisection to depth n.
  • (digits := d) first tries the digit evaluator of #cas [N d] at a matching precision and prints d decimal places.
  • set_option cega.maxPrecision (default 256) and cega.maxRefinementWork (default 4096) cap the precision and the work of a subdivision.
  • Under set_option cas.suggest true the report also offers the first checked step above as an example to paste in place of the command, when the binders and the type of that example, elaborated where the command is with the variables of its section, are the proposition of the step up to unfolding instances, and the whole example elaborates there without errors to a declaration of that proposition with no sorry (cas.suggest).

Examples

#cas [enclose x in [0, 1]] (x ^ 2 + x)

Output (certified interval in ℝ): [0, 2]
Upper bound: 2
Absolute bound: 2
Center and radius: 1 ± 1

#cas [enclose x in [0, 1], y in [0, 1]] (x * y + sin y)

Output (certified interval in ℝ): [0, 1.841471]

#cas [enclose x in [-2, 2]] (x / (1 + x ^ 2))

Output (certified interval in ℝ): [-2, 2]

#cas (depth := 2) [enclose x in [-2, 2]] (x / (1 + x ^ 2))

Output (certified interval in ℝ): [-1/2, 1/2]

Bisection to depth 2 cuts [-2, 2] at 0 and at the turning points ±1, so x / (1 + x ^ 2) is monotone on each piece and the enclosure is its exact range.

#cas [enclose] (1 / 1000000000000000000000000)

Output (certified interval in ℝ): [0.000000, 0.000001]
Upper bound: 0.000001
Absolute bound: 0.000001
Center and radius: ≈0.000000 ± 0.000001

The exact value 1/1000000000000000000000000 is longer than 24 characters, so the bounds are rounded outward to 6 decimal places. The center is rounded down and marked ≈, and the radius covers that rounding, as in the theorem |e - 0.000000| ≤ 0.000001.

In a proof

theorem enclose_bound (x : ℝ) (h₀ : 0 ≤ x) (h₁ : x ≤ 1) : x ^ 2 + x ≤ 2 := by
  cas

The tactics cas and cega take the box from the hypotheses on x.

See also

Mathematica Interval, SymPy AccumBounds. The modes N, minimize and maximize, and the tactic cega [enclose ...], which proves a goal from the same query. Oracle route: #cas [enclose x in [a, b], oracle := gappa] e (in CASOracle), which proves the enclosure that the oracle proposes, rounded outward.

Possible issues

#cas [enclose x in [-1, 1]] (1 / x)

no checked interval route succeeded on this box. Possible domain obstruction: check whether
denominator intervals exclude zero.

1 / x is unbounded near 0, so no interval holds its values on [-1, 1]. Enclose it on boxes that exclude zero, such as [1/10, 1].

#cas [enclose x in [0, pi]] (sin x)

interval endpoints must be exact rational literals, such as -1, 3/2, -1/10, or 0.1

Use a rational interval that contains the one you mean, such as [0, 315/100] for [0, π].

#cas [enclose x in [1, 0]] (x)

interval endpoints are reversed: 1 > 0

Write the smaller endpoint first.

#cas [integrate x] e finds an antiderivative of e with respect to x, checks it by differentiation, and prints it with the conditions under which it holds.

Theorem

For the printed antiderivative F and the checked conditions c₁, …, cₖ, which the Conditions line prints in its display form, the first checked step proves the fundamental theorem of calculus about Mathlib's real functions, ∀ a b : ℝ, (∀ x ∈ Set.uIcc a b, c₁ ∧ … ∧ cₖ) → ∫ x in a..b, e = F b - F a, for every value of the other variables, such as ∀ (a b : ℝ), ∫ (x : ℝ) in a..b, x * Real.exp x = Real.exp b * (b - 1) - Real.exp a * (a - 1) for #cas [integrate x] (x * exp x). The lemma CAS.IntegrationCheck.AntiderivativeCert.intervalIntegral_eq_sub_of_line transports it from the checked certificate, whose statements for the internal expression syntax follow it (CAS.IntegrationCheck.AntiderivativeCert.intervalIntegral_eq_sub_eval_add_smul_single). The first step is shown when its proof succeeds within its own budget of maxHeartbeats heartbeats; otherwise the report keeps only the internal statements. The limits get other names when a variable is called a or b. The tactic cas proves HasDerivAt (fun x ↦ F) e x, ∫ x in a..b, e = v and, over a half-line D, IntegrableOn (fun x ↦ e) D ∧ ∫ x in D, e = v.

Conditions and limits

e uses the functions of #cas [derive x], and the other variables are parameters. The search covers polynomials and the table of elementary antiderivatives, substitution, rational functions, integration by parts, polynomials times exponential and trigonometric phases, and rational functions of sin and cos; the backends registered with @[cas_route integrate], such as the Gaussian integrals, run first. The search is bounded, and a candidate is printed only after its derivative is checked. The rational planner splits off powers of x but does not factor a general polynomial. It can still integrate a logarithmic derivative or a proper fraction over x^4 + a*x^2 + 1 for -2 < a < 2.

Options

Under set_option cas.verbose true the first computation step also shows the tree of differentiation rules of the antiderivative, each rule with its input and its raw derivative. Under set_option cas.suggest true the report also offers the first checked step above as an example to paste in place of the command, when the binders and the type of that example, elaborated where the command is with the variables of its section, are the proposition of the step up to unfolding instances, and the whole example elaborates there without errors to a declaration of that proposition with no sorry (cas.suggest).

Examples

#cas [grad x, y, …] e computes the gradient of e in the listed variables, in that order, and prints it as a vector.

Theorem

For the variables x₁, …, xₙ of e, the printed components g₁, …, gₙ and the checked conditions c₁, …, cₖ, which the Conditions line prints in its display form, the first checked step proves ∀ x₁ … xₙ : ℝ, c₁ → … → cₖ → HasGradientAt (fun p ↦ e) !₂[g₁, …, gₙ] !₂[x₁, …, xₙ] about Mathlib's real functions, with e written in the coordinates p.ofLp 0, … of EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n), such as ∀ (x y : ℝ), HasGradientAt (fun p ↦ p.ofLp 0 * p.ofLp 1) !₂[y, x] !₂[x, y] for #cas [grad x, y] (x * y). The lemma CAS.Verified.Expr.hasGradientAt_of_closedGradient transports it from the symbolic gradient, fixed by one kernel decision. The first step is shown when its proof succeeds within its own budget of maxHeartbeats heartbeats. Each component is also proved as by #cas [derive x], and the vector of the components is gradient (fun y ↦ eval y e) p, Mathlib's gradient of the evaluation of e in the internal expression syntax, at every point p of ℝ^n where e satisfies CAS.Verified.Expr.ValidAt: every divisor and every argument of log is nonzero, every argument of sqrt and every base of a real power is positive, and no argument of asin or acos is 1 or -1 (CAS.Verified.Expr.closedGradient_eval_eq_gradient).

Conditions and limits

Every variable of e must be listed. The functions are those of #cas [derive x], and the conditions are the validity conditions of e.

Options

Under set_option cas.verbose true the details of each component also show the tree of differentiation rules, as for #cas [derive x].

Examples

#cas [grad x, y] (x ^ 2 * y + y ^ 3)

Output (vector ℝ^2; order x, y): (2*x*y, x^2 + 3*y^2)

#cas [grad x, y] (sin (x * y))

Output (vector ℝ^2; order x, y): (cos(x*y)*y, cos(x*y)*x)

theorem grad_first_component (x y : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (fun x ↦ x ^ 2 * y + y ^ 3) (2 * x * y) x := by
  cas

#cas [simplify] e simplifies the real expression e by checked exact rewrites and prints the result with the conditions under which it equals e.

Theorem

For the variables x₁, …, xₙ of e, the printed result e' and the checked conditions c₁, …, cₖ, which the Conditions line prints in its display form, the first checked step proves ∀ x₁ … xₙ : ℝ, c₁ → … → cₖ → e = e' about Mathlib's real functions, such as ∀ (x : ℝ), x + x = 2 * x for #cas [simplify] (x + x). The lemma CAS.Command.eq_of_simplifyFinDisplayRoute transports it from the statement for the internal expression syntax (CAS.Verified.Expr.SideClaimRoute.sound), which follows it among the checked steps. The first step is shown when its proof succeeds within its own budget of maxHeartbeats heartbeats; otherwise the report keeps only the internal statement. The tactic cas proves the same identity.

Conditions and limits

The variables of e are real. The functions are abs, sin, cos, tan, sinh, cosh, tanh, atan, asin, acos, exp, log and sqrt, with +, -, *, / and powers; a power with a variable exponent is a real power. Cancelling a divisor d adds the condition d ≠ 0, and combining real powers of a adds the condition a > 0.

Options

Under set_option cas.suggest true the report also offers the first checked step above as an example to paste in place of the command, when the binders and the type of that example, elaborated where the command is with the variables of its section, are the proposition of the step up to unfolding instances, and the whole example elaborates there without errors to a declaration of that proposition with no sorry (cas.suggest).

Examples

#cas [simplify] ((x ^ 4 - 1) / (x ^ 2 - 1))

Output (scalar ℝ): x^2 + 1
Conditions: x^2 - 1 ≠ 0

#cas [simplify] (exp ((x^2 - y^2)/(x - y)))

Output (scalar ℝ): exp(x + y)
Conditions: x - y ≠ 0

#cas [simplify] (a ^ p * a * sqrt a / a ^ q)

Output (scalar ℝ): a^(p - q + 3/2)
Conditions: a > 0

In a proof

theorem simplify_quotient (x : ℝ) (h : x ^ 2 - 1 ≠ 0) :
    (x ^ 4 - 1) / (x ^ 2 - 1) = x ^ 2 + 1 := by
  cas

See also

Mathematica Simplify, SymPy simplify. The modes fullSimplify, together, cancel and factor, and the tactic cas.

asin/arcsin, acos/arccos, exp, log, or sqrt. If multiplication was intended, write it explicitly
with `*`

An identifier applied to an argument is read as a function. Write a product as x * y.

#cas [simplify] ((1 / (1/x + 1/(1-x)) - 1) / (1 / (1/x + 1/(1-x)) - 1))

Output (scalar ℝ): 1
Conditions: 1/(1/x + 1/(1 - x)) - 1 ≠ 0

A condition is written as a polynomial in descending powers only when it equals that polynomial for every value of its variables. The divisor here equals -(x^2 - x + 1) only for x ≠ 0 and x ≠ 1 (at x = 0 it is 0, since 1/0 = 0), so the condition keeps the form of the input.

The direct method gives a unique weak solution of the odd-power Dirichlet equation

-Delta u + linear * u + nonlinear * u ^ (2 * k + 1) = f.

The analytic hypotheses require integrability of the potential energy, an L² representative N u of the polynomial nonlinearity for every u ∈ H¹₀, and Fréchet differentiability of the integral potential with derivative loadFunctional (N u). The theorem assumes these inputs; it does not derive them from a dimension or exponent restriction. By Sobolev embedding the representability hNrep holds for every k when n ≤ 2, and for 2 * k + 1 ≤ n / (n - 2) when n ≥ 3. Above that range, with nonlinear ≠ 0 and Ω open and nonempty, it fails and the theorem is vacuous.

For two parameters θ and θ' that agree on the boundary of Ω, the integral over Ω of the density of the member through each point plus the pairing of the family flux with the differential of the parameter has the same value. On Ω the integrand is the density of U 0 plus the divergence of the calibration field, and the integral of the divergence depends on the boundary values of the parameter only.

Independence of the surface through a given boundary curve. Under the hypotheses of multipleIntegral_independence on the family, suppose that over every boundary point the surfaces of the family do not meet: t ↦ Z t x is injective on J. If the surfaces z(x) = Z (θ x) x and z'(x) = Z (θ' x) x have the same boundary values, J* has the same value along both. This is Hilbert's statement, "independent of the choice of the surface passing through the given closed twisted curve", for the parameter graphs of the family.

Equal boundary values and injectivity give equal parameters on the boundary. Without injectivity the conclusion can fail.

Hilbert's independence theorem for a multiple integral, for a family of extremal surfaces. Let Ω be a bounded open set with C¹ graph boundary, and let z = Z t, t ∈ J, be solutions of the Euler–Lagrange system of ∫ F(Dz, z; x) dx on Ω (IsExtremalFamily). Let θ and θ' be C¹ functions with values in J (IsGraphParameter) that agree on the boundary of Ω; then the surfaces z(x) = Z (θ x) x and z'(x) = Z (θ' x) x pass through the same boundary curve. The integral J* = ∫ {F(P) + (Dz - P) F_P(P)} dω has the same value along the two surfaces. Both integrands are integrable (integrableOn_fieldIntegrand).

This is ExtremalFamily.integral_invariant_eq_of_eqOn_frontier, through integral_fieldIntegrand.

Lax–Milgram with inhomogeneous data. Let ι : V → U map a Hilbert space into an additive group, and let B u v be additive in the state u ∈ U, with B (ι w) v = B₀ w v for a coercive bounded form B₀ on V and B g v = ℓg v for a continuous functional ℓg. Hilbert's inequality. For two variables, a uniformly regular integrand satisfies F_pp > 0 and F_pp F_qq - F_pq² > 0 at every point, where F_pp, F_pq and F_qq are the second derivatives of F in the two coordinate directions. So it defines a regular variation problem in Hilbert's sense, with a positive definite second derivative.

With a = F_pp, c = F_qq, d = F_pq the lower bound says that (a - θ) s² + 2 d s t + (c - θ) t² ≥ 0 for all s, t. Hence d² ≤ (a - θ)(c - θ), and a c - d² ≥ θ (a + c) - θ² ≥ θ².

Hölder continuous gradient of local minimizers (De Giorgi–Nash regularity). In every dimension n and for all θ > 0 and Λ there is an exponent γ in (0, 1) with the following property. Let Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ be open, let F be C² with θ ‖ξ‖² ≤ D²F(p)(ξ, ξ) ≤ Λ ‖ξ‖² for all p and ξ, and let u in W^{1,2}_loc(Ω) be a local minimizer of ∫ F(∇u). Then u has a representative v that is C¹ on Ω, and every point of Ω is the centre of a ball on which ∇v is Hölder continuous with exponent γ.

This is the first step of the regularity theory of minimizers (De Giorgi, Nash): a C² density gives C^{1,γ} locally. The Hölder condition is stated for the gradient as a map into ℝⁿ. The statement is exists_contDiffOn_one_of_isLocalMinimizerOn together with exists_holder_exponent_gradient_of_isLocalMinimizerOn.

PDE.CalculusOfVariations.IsLocalMinimizerOn {n : ℕ} (F : ℝ^n → ℝ) (Ω : Set ℝ^n) (u : ℝ^n → ℝ) : Prop

u is a local minimizer of ∫ F(∇u) on Ω: on every open V with compact closure in Ω, every W^{1,2}(V) element that represents u has no more energy than its perturbation by any smooth function with compact support in V.

The perturbations may be large, and they are the smallest class in use, so among the notions that compare with all perturbations in a class this is the weakest. Nothing is asked of u outside such sets V, and Ω need not be bounded.

The predicate does not say that u is in W^{1,2}_loc(Ω): on a set V where u has no representative in W^{1,2}(V) it asks nothing. It does not say that the energies are finite either: the integrals are Bochner integrals, which are 0 for a density that is not integrable. The regularity theorems assume IsLocallyWkpOn 1 2 Ω u and a density with Lipschitz gradient, for which every energy is finite (integrable_gradientDensity_of_lipschitzWith).

Here 1 < p < ∞, the domain is bounded and measurable, and its dimension is positive. On open domains this is the usual affine W¹ᵖ₀ boundary class; on measurable sets the condition means the supported smooth-core closure.

HasSum.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} [AddCommMonoid α] [TopologicalSpace α] (f : β → α) (a : α) (L : SummationFilter β := SummationFilter.unconditional β) : Prop

HasSum f a L means that the (potentially infinite) sum of the f b for b : β converges to a along the SummationFilter L.

By default L is the unconditional one, corresponding to the limit of all finite sets towards the entire type. So we take the sum over bigger and bigger finite sets. This sum operation is invariant under permuting the terms (while sums for more general summation filters usually are not). This is based on Mario Carneiro's infinite sum df-tsms in Metamath.

In particular, the function ℕ → ℝ sending n to (-1) ^ n / (n + 1) does not have a sum for this definition, although it is summable for the conditional summation filter that takes limits of sums over n ∈ {0, ..., X} as X → ∞. However, a series which is absolutely convergent with respect to the conditional summation filter is in fact unconditionally summable.

For the definition and many statements, α does not need to be a topological additive monoid, only an additive monoid with a topology (i.e. the addition is not assumed to be continuous). We only add this assumption later, for the lemmas where it is relevant.

Pressure-free Leray-Hopf solution on [0,T].

The weak momentum equation and incompressibility come from WeakSolution. The additional fields give velocity and gradient Bochner bounds, continuity into the weak topology of L², the initial trace as equality of L² classes, force-work integrability, and the all-time energy inequality measured from the prescribed datum.

The initial datum is required only in L². Spatial-gradient membership and its weak derivative identity are imposed on (0,T], while the velocity and its initial trace are defined on [0,T]. These representative requirements at every positive time are stronger than an almost-everywhere formulation.

7624:
cega proves real inequalities on boxes, closed numerical bounds, bounds on interval integrals and closed statements about floats from certificates that the kernel checks.

Theorem

cega closes goals of these shapes, with closed bounds a, b and c:

  • f x ≤ c, f x < c, c ≤ f x, c < f x, |f x| ≤ c and |f x| < c;
  • a ≤ f x ∧ f x ≤ b, also with <, and f x ∈ Set.Icc a b, also with Set.Ioo, Set.Ico and Set.Ioc;
  • f x ≤ g x, and conjunctions of these goals;
  • bounds on one interval integral, such as (∫ x in a..b, f x) ≤ c and |(∫ x in a..b, f x) - c| ≤ ε, with rational limits;
  • the certificate propositions EnclosedOn, BoundOn, ApproxOn and ResidualBound on a box;
  • the real and nonnegative real inequalities that FloatLib's interval proves, with finite sums, norms, dot and matrix products, and the bounds over a whole domain that it reads: ∀ u : ℝ, … for a trigonometric polynomial, ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc lo hi, … and ∀ z : ℂ, ‖z‖ = 1 → …;
  • closed decidable statements about floats, such as (1.5 : Binary64) + 2.25 = 3.75, decided in the kernel as float_decide decides them.

On a box, every real variable is bounded by hypotheses a ≤ x and x ≤ b, x ∈ Set.Icc a b or |x| ≤ r with rational literals; a goal without variables needs none.

Conditions and limits

The routes run in this order, each only on goals of its shape: a checked carrier of the goal, float_decide, the quadrature of an integral, a certificate goal, the box route, FloatLib's interval, dyadic_interval on a closed goal, and a kernel certificate for a closed decidable proposition that is not about floats. The box route first tries FloatLib's check, which refutes the negation of the stated bounds on pieces of the box that cega chooses, by FloatLib's interval evaluation checked in the kernel. When that falls short, it encloses the expressions of the goal on the box of the hypotheses and compares the enclosure with the bound by exact rational arithmetic; when the first enclosure is too weak, it subdivides the box to depth 2. An integral bound uses Simpson panels when the domain checker certifies the first four derivatives of the integrand on [a, b], and range panels, which need only continuity, otherwise or when the Simpson panels fall short; the panel count doubles from 1 up to cega.maxIntegrationPanels. interval reads the bounds in the hypotheses itself, with FloatLib's defaults unless (prec := n), (digits := d) or (depth := n) sets them, and dyadic_interval runs at 32 bits unless (prec := n) or (digits := d) sets them. The functions of the box route are those of the grammar of #cas [N d], written as Mathlib terms such as Real.sin x and Real.sqrt x, and a box has at most 8 variables (cega.maxDimension). A false bound, or a true one that the enclosures do not reach, is refused with the next call to try; for an integral the message gives the interval that the panel search proposes.

Options

  • [use_floats] computes the enclosures of the box route with IEEE floats of the format binary64, rounded outward and checked in the kernel, instead of exact rationals; [use_floats := false] is the default. (arith := F) chooses the format F, an IEEE binary format of FloatLib such as binary32 or binary128, and set_option cega.arithmetic "binary64" sets the arithmetic of a section.
  • (prec := n), (expOrder := n), (logTerms := n) and (sqrtDigits := n) set the precision of the box query as in #cas [enclose]; (prec := n) also sets the endpoint bits of interval and the bits of a closed goal, and (digits := d) gives both about 3.3 d + 8 bits.
  • (depth := n) sets the depth of the subdivision tried after the first query, default 2, and the subdivision depth of interval, which is otherwise FloatLib's default.
  • (panels := n) fixes the panel count of an integral bound; (digits := d) fixes its working precision.
  • set_option cega.maxIntegrationPanels n caps the doubling of the panels, default 256.
  • set_option cega.nativeCertificates true lets cega [fast] check finite certificates with compiled code, which also trusts Lean's compiler; the default false keeps every check in the kernel.

Examples

example (x : ℝ) (h₀ : 0 ≤ x) (h₁ : x ≤ 1) : Real.sin x ≤ 0.85 := by
  cega

example : Real.exp 1 ≤ 2.72 := by
  cega

example : (∫ x in (0 : ℝ)..1, Real.exp (-x ^ 2)) ≤ 3 / 4 := by
  cega

example (x : Fin 3 → ℝ) (hx : ∀ i, x i ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) : ∑ i, x i ^ 2 ≤ 3 := by
  cega

In a proof

theorem cega_sin_lt_one (x : ℝ) (h₀ : 0 ≤ x) (h₁ : x ≤ 1) : Real.sin x < 1 := by
  have h : Real.sin x ≤ 17 / 20 := by cega
  linarith

See also

Mathematica Interval and NIntegrate, SymPy AccumBounds. The tactics cega? and cas, which tries cega on ordinary inequalities, and the modes enclose, nintegrate and N.

Possible issues

example (x : ℝ) (h₀ : 0 ≤ x) (h₁ : x ≤ 1) : Real.sin x ≤ 0.8 := by
  cega

cega box route: comparison with the stated bound: the certified value does not give the stated
bound.

The bound is false, since Real.sin 1 > 0.84. For a true bound that the enclosure misses, the message proposes cega (depth := 4) or cega (prec := 24).

example (x : ℝ) : x * (1 - x) ≤ 1 / 4 := by
  cega

cega box route: no rational bounds on `x` in the hypotheses; the route needs hypotheses `a ≤ x` and
`x ≤ b`, `x ∈ Set.Icc a b`, or `|x| ≤ r` with rational literal endpoints

Add bounds on x as hypotheses. A bound for every x, as here, follows from nlinarith [sq_nonneg (2 * x - 1)].

Extensions:

  • cega [fast]

    Try float_decide on a closed statement about floats, checked in the kernel, then closed finite and polynomial certificates under the cega.nativeCertificates checking profile, then the kernel routes of bare cega. A native certificate also trusts Lean's compiler and runtime; with the default profile, cega.nativeCertificates = false, it is bare cega.

  • cega [use_floats]

    Bare cega with the enclosures of its box route computed in IEEE floating-point arithmetic: cega [use_floats] and cega [use_floats := true] in binary64, or in the format of the option cega.arithmetic where it names one, cega [use_floats] (arith := F) in the IEEE binary format F of FloatLib, and cega [use_floats := false] in exact arithmetic, the default. Every lower end is rounded toward -∞ and every upper end toward +∞, the kernel evaluates the float operations, and the theorem is about real numbers. The items (depth := n) and (arith := F) follow the bracket group, and fast may share it. A float computation that does not prove the goal fails, with the format and the reason.

  • cega (prec := n) (depth := n) (panels := n)

    Bare cega with a precision policy for its box route: (prec := n) and the other items of the explicit form set the precision of the query, and (depth := n) the depth of the subdivision that bare cega tries when the first query does not prove the bound (two by default). As in the explicit form, depth zero still bisects the box once. (prec := n), (digits := d) and (depth := n) also set the endpoint bits and the subdivision depth of FloatLib's interval, the route after the box route. On an interval integral, (panels := n) fixes the number of quadrature panels, which otherwise doubles from one until the bound holds, up to the option cega.maxIntegrationPanels.

  • cega [enclose ...] expr

    Synthesize a certificate for expr on an exact rational box and use it to close the current goal. The goal selects the projection: an enclosure for EnclosedOn f s lo hi, an upper bound for BoundOn f s c, an absolute bound for BoundOn (fun x ↦ |f x|) s c, a midpoint approximation for ApproxOn f (fun _ ↦ c) s ε, and the bound an ordinary goal on the box's variables states (f x ≤ c, c ≤ f x, |f x| ≤ c, a ≤ f x ∧ f x ≤ b, f x ∈ Set.Icc a b). The optional configuration group, for example (prec := 40), selects the numerical precision policy, and (depth := n) encloses after n levels of checked box refinement. (arith := F) computes the enclosure with IEEE floats of the format F of FloatLib, as in cega (arith := binary64) [enclose x in [0, 1]] (Real.exp x), and (arith := "exact") with exact rationals whatever the option cega.arithmetic is; the flag use_floats belongs to bare cega. An empty coordinate list, as in cega [enclose] Real.sqrt 2, queries a closed expression.

  • cega using carrier

    Close the goal by projecting one explicitly supplied checked CEGA carrier.

PseudoMetricSpace.{u} (α : Type u) : Type u

A pseudometric space is a type endowed with a ℝ-valued distance dist satisfying reflexivity dist x x = 0, commutativity dist x y = dist y x, and the triangle inequality dist x z ≤ dist x y + dist y z.

Note that we do not require dist x y = 0 → x = y. See metric spaces (MetricSpace) for the similar class with that stronger assumption.

Any pseudometric space is a topological space and a uniform space (see TopologicalSpace, UniformSpace), where the topology and uniformity come from the metric. Note that a T1 pseudometric space is just a metric space.

We make the uniformity/topology part of the data instead of deriving it from the metric. This e.g. ensures that we do not get a diamond when doing [PseudoMetricSpace α] [PseudoMetricSpace β] : TopologicalSpace (α × β): The product metric and product topology agree, but not definitionally so. See Note [forgetful inheritance].

Set.univ.{u} {α : Type u} : Set α

The universal set on a type α is the set containing all elements of α.

This is conceptually the "same as" α (in set theory, it is actually the same), but type theory makes the distinction that α is a type while Set.univ is a term of type Set α. Set.univ can itself be coerced to a type ↥Set.univ which is in bijection with (but distinct from) α.

Fin.rev {n : ℕ} (i : Fin n) : Fin n

Replaces a value with its difference from the largest value in the type.

Considering the values of Fin n as a sequence 0, 1, …, n-2, n-1, Fin.rev finds the corresponding element of the reversed sequence. In other words, it maps 0 to n-1, 1 to n-2, ..., and n-1 to 0.

Examples:

  • (5 : Fin 6).rev = (0 : Fin 6)
  • (0 : Fin 6).rev = (5 : Fin 6)
  • (2 : Fin 5).rev = (2 : Fin 5)

Eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → Prop

The equality relation. It has one introduction rule, Eq.refl. We use a = b as notation for Eq a b. A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.

variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd

Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value. That is, given h1 : a = b and h2 : p a, we can construct a proof for p b using substitution: Eq.subst h1 h2. Example:

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2

The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of Eq.subst and Eq.symm, and you can enter it by typing \t. For more information: Equality

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

  • The recommended spelling of = in identifiers is eq.

The domain is open, both u and flux ∘ u are locally integrable there, and the distributional identity

∫ (u φ_t + flux(u) φ_x) = 0

holds for every compactly supported C¹ test function. The displayed integrand is integrable because both coefficients are locally integrable and the derivatives of the test function are continuous and compactly supported in the domain.

This is the interior distributional equation on U. It is not the weak half-space initial-value formulation: no initial datum or boundary term at t = 0 is part of this structure.

ContDiffWithinAt.{u, uE, uF} (𝕜 : Type u) [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {E : Type uE} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type uF} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] (n : WithTop ℕ∞) (f : E → F) (s : Set E) (x : E) : Prop

A function is continuously differentiable up to order n within a set s at a point x if it admits continuous derivatives up to order n in a neighborhood of x in s ∪ {x}. The parameter n belongs to ℕ∞ω (accessible in the ContDiff scope), i.e. it can be a natural number, ∞, or ω. For n = ∞, we only require that this holds up to any finite order (where the neighborhood may depend on the finite order we consider). For n = ω, we require the function to be analytic within s at x. The precise definition we give (all the derivatives should be analytic) is more involved to work around issues when the space is not complete, but it is equivalent when the space is complete.

For instance, a real function which is C^m on (-1/m, 1/m) for each natural m, but not better, is C^∞ at 0 within univ.

This theorem combines the exact global balance, the integrated production bound, and Mathlib's Grönwall inequality. Every analytic assumption used by those steps is a hypothesis: continuity of total energy, local dominated differentiation, pointwise PDE and coefficient regularity, integrable forcing, and compactly supported C¹ flux slices. It does not construct a solution or establish the hypotheses.

Local C² boundary and value data give a C² classical solution for a Hamiltonian that is C² only near the compatible noncharacteristic initial phase.

A global representative of the Hamiltonian's germ supplies the constructed momentum field and flow. Its solution has Du(boundary(y0))=p0. Continuity of (Du,u,x) then gives a smaller open solution neighborhood on which the representative agrees with the original Hamiltonian. The boundary neighborhood is also restricted, retaining its value trace and the requested ambient domain. This is a local existence theorem, with no uniqueness conclusion.

Evans, §3.2.4: local existence from a regular characteristic flow.

Given compatible boundary gradients, a noncharacteristic basepoint, and the regular characteristic flow of (31), there are open neighborhoods W₀ of the boundary parameter and V of the boundary point together with a C² function u such that

  • F(Du,u,x)=0 on V,
  • u(boundary(y))=data(y) and Du(boundary(y))=initialGradient(y) for y∈W₀, and
  • every point of V lies in the requested ambient domain Ω.

Both the residual and Du = p are derived from the characteristic and first-variation ODEs. The identity Du = p ∘ coords then gives a C¹ derivative, hence the C² regularity in Evans's Theorem 2. This theorem takes a regular characteristic flow as input; SmoothConstruction constructs that flow from boundary and value data.

contact_evolution is not the desired gradient identity. It is the homogeneous linearized characteristic ODE

Wrapper for adding elementary propositions to the type class systems. Warning: this can easily be abused. See the rest of this docstring for details.

Certain propositions should not be treated as a class globally, but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system in specific circumstances.

For example, ZMod p is a field if and only if p is a prime number. In order to be able to find this field instance automatically by type class search, we have to turn p.Prime into an instance implicit assumption.

On the other hand, making Nat.Prime a class would require a major refactoring of the library, and it is questionable whether making Nat.Prime a class is desirable at all. The compromise is to add the assumption [Fact p.Prime] to ZMod.instField.

In particular, this class is not intended for turning the type class system into an automated theorem prover for first-order logic.

Evans, §7.2.3: the elliptic step in Theorem 5(ii).

Assume the divergence-form weak wave identity holds almost everywhere in time and that both f(t) and u_{tt}(t) are essentially bounded in L²(Omega). On a domain carrying the operational C2BoundaryAtlas, assume uniformly elliptic W¹,∞ principal coefficients with global C¹ representatives. The wave trajectory then has a canonical L∞_t H²_x representative. Constructing the atlas from an ordinary geometric C² boundary is not part of this theorem.

The pointwise estimate retained by the theorem is

‖u(t)‖_{H²} ≤ ‖S₂‖ (C_f + C_tt),

where S₂ : L²(Omega) → H²(Omega) is the global elliptic solution operator. This is the operator form of Evans's estimates (59)-(60). In particular, the constant is independent of the Galerkin dimension and of time.

Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 5(ii): identification of the differentiated Galerkin limits.

Suppose one common filter gives weak limits for an original Galerkin family and its differentiated family. The exact finite-dimensional identities

J (duₘ) = velocityₘ,

J* (dvelocityₘ) = accelerationₘ

then survive weak convergence. If the coefficient derivative identity d uₘ/dt = duₘ is also retained in the identity Gelfand triple, the limit du is the V-valued weak derivative of u.

Uniform essential bounds on duₘ in V and dvelocityₘ in H pass to the same limits by weak closedness of the almost-everywhere norm balls. Finally, for an autonomous operator and weakly differentiable forcing, the theorem constructs u_{ttt} in L²(a,b;V*).

Evans Section 7.2.3: differentiated Galerkin limit with bounded nonsymmetric lower-order terms.

Let the autonomous wave operator split as B = A + R. The principal part A is symmetric and coercive on the energy space, while R is allowed to be nonsymmetric and is controlled in the mixed V x H norm. Stable dense trial projections, compatible ambient initial data, a coherent forcing chain, and the uniform forcing budget generate a finite chain of ambient weak-wave solutions for the full operator A + R, provided hRitz holds:

(A + R) (q r.succ - P_k (q r.succ)) w = 0

for every trial level k, adjacent jet index r, and test w in that trial space. Here P_k is the restriction of the stable pivot projection to V. This full-operator condition is separate from stability and density.

All finite-dimensional trajectories, their uniform bounds, and their common weak limit are constructed in the proof. In particular, no limiting weak wave or higher-regularity conclusion is included among the hypotheses.

Module.finrank.{u_1, u_2} (R : Type u_1) (M : Type u_2) [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M] : ℕ

The rank of a module as a natural number.

For a finite-dimensional vector space V over a field k, Module.finrank k V is equal to the dimension of V over k.

For a general module M over a ring R, Module.finrank R M is defined to be the supremum of the cardinalities of the R-linearly independent subsets of M, if this supremum is finite. It is defined by convention to be 0 if this supremum is infinite. See Module.rank for a cardinal-valued version where infinite rank modules have rank an infinite cardinal.

Note that if R is not a field then there can exist modules M with ¬(Module.Finite R M) but finrank R M ≠ 0. For example ℚ has finrank equal to 1 over ℤ, because the nonempty ℤ-linearly independent subsets of ℚ are precisely the nonzero singletons.

The recursive derivative data underlying an order-m Sobolev time jet.

At order zero there is only an L²_t L²_x trajectory. At successor order, the head is H^{m+1}-valued, its weak time derivative is an H^m-valued trajectory, and that derivative itself carries the remaining order-m jet. The canonical map H^{m+1} → H^m is inserted before stating the weak derivative identity in the identity Gelfand triple on H^m.

This is an ordinary Hilbert-valued weak derivative, not an additional PDE assumption. The Gelfand form is used because the Lions-Magenes theorem then supplies the canonical representative continuous through both time endpoints.

This recursive shape avoids storing the same analytic object at unrelated dependent indices. It makes the induction in Evans literal: differentiating once means taking the recursive tail.

Unlike eq_of_evans_coefficients, this theorem has no scalar IntervalIntegrable hypotheses. The L² solution types and homogeneous weak equation provide integrability of B(u,v), hence of A(u,v)=B(u,v)-R(u,v). In concrete divergence form it follows from measurability of the coefficient fields. hAdotBound follows from uniform bounds on the time derivative of the principal coefficients. hRBound puts the H norm on the solution slot, so it follows from uniform bounds on c, b and div b after a spatial integration by parts; bounds on b alone do not give it.

Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 5(i): abstract Galerkin form.

Assume a bounded projected Galerkin family with the same exact initial displacement q₀ and velocity p₀ at every index. Suppose in addition that estimate (52) has supplied dimension-independent essential bounds

‖uₘ(t)‖_V ≤ Cᵤ and ‖uₘ'(t)‖_H ≤ Cᵥ.

Then the compactness construction produces a weak solution satisfying

u ∈ L∞(a,b;V) and u_t ∈ L∞(a,b;H),

with the same almost-everywhere bounds. In concrete divergence-form wave problems, ae_norm_displacementLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le and ae_norm_velocityLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le supply these two additional hypotheses from the coercive Galerkin energy estimate.

The proof uses the same common ultrafilter for displacement, velocity, and acceleration. The weak-wave equations are passed to the limit exactly as in exists_of_bounded_projected_galerkin_family, while improvedRegularity_of_weak_L2_limits preserves the closed convex essential norm balls. Thus the regularity conclusion is proved rather than stored as extra data in the definition of a weak solution.

The projected Galerkin spatial equations are closed under Evans's weak compactness limit.

At level n, the acceleration is only the residual precomposed with the trial projection:

accelerationₙ = (ell - B(·)uₙ) ∘ Pₙ.

This is the finite-dimensional statement: in general a Galerkin approximation does not solve the ambient equation in all of V*. Uniform energy stability and Pₙv → v imply strong convergence of the lifted projections on L²(V). Pairing the weakly convergent residuals against those strongly convergent tests identifies the acceleration limit with ell - B(·)u, and hence recovers the full ambient equation only at the limit.

Weak sequential/net closure of Evans's weak-wave solution predicate.

Suppose a family of weak-wave solutions has a common weak limit in the three natural Bochner spaces:

  • displacement in L²(a,b;V),
  • velocity in L²(a,b;H), and
  • acceleration in L²(a,b;V*).

The acceleration convergence is stated after Riesz transport, matching the Hilbert weak topology used by the compactness theorem. Then the three limit objects again satisfy the weak-wave predicate with the same initial data and forcing.

The proof follows the Evans limit passage:

  1. bounded linearity of H → V* passes the displacement identity;
  2. fixed space-time testing passes the velocity identity; and
  3. bounded operator-valued multiplication passes B(t)u weakly, so uniqueness of weak limits yields u_tt + B(t)u = ell in L²(V*).

Write V = H¹₀(Ω), H = L²(Ω), and suppose operatorBound bounds the autonomous principal form. Set

energyBudget = operatorBound ‖uInit‖² + 2 ‖f‖².

For any coercivity constant coercivityConstant > 0 of the form, the theorem constructs the weak solution u, its pivot derivative ut, and the spatial H² lift h2Lift, and proves

ess sup_t ‖u(t)‖_V ≤ sqrt (energyBudget / coercivityConstant),

‖ut‖_{L²_t H} ≤ sqrt energyBudget,

Time regularity for an arbitrary Bochner L²(H) forcing.

For bounded continuous pivot loads the measurable Carathéodory solver constructs the Galerkin family internally. The improved Galerkin estimate uses only the load's L² norm, so density and coercive completion pass both the solution and its L²(H) time derivative to an arbitrary Bochner load. The functions A, Adot, and R are fixed across these forcing approximations, and A remains time-dependent in the limiting equation. The derivative bound N of the principal form contributes N/2 beside the remainder's coefficient L² in the energy budget. Principal coercivity gives the L∞(V) bound; coercivity of the full form supplies the basic L²(V) estimate and continuous dependence on the load.

The dimension-independent Galerkin estimate of steps 1 and 2 in the proof of Evans §7.1.3, Theorem 5.

Write the time-dependent form as an autonomous symmetric principal part plus a lower-order remainder,

B(t) = A + R(t).

Assume the forcing is represented in the pivot space and the remainder has the mixed bound

|R(t)(u,v)| ≤ L ‖u‖_V ‖Jv‖_H.

Testing the almost-everywhere Galerkin equation with the coefficient derivative and using symmetry of A gives, on every prefix [a,t],

(1/2) A(u(t),u(t)) + (1/2) ∫ ‖Ju'‖² ≤ (1/2) A(u(a),u(a)) + ∫ (‖f‖² + L² ‖u‖²).

The constants are independent of the trial space. With coercivity of A and the basic Galerkin estimate, this gives uniform L∞(a,b;V) and L²(a,b;H)-derivative bounds.

Abstract Hilbert-space Aubin–Lions compactness.

Let V ↪ H be a compact Gelfand inclusion and let a family of trajectories be uniformly bounded in L²(a,b;V), with dual time derivatives uniformly bounded in L²(a,b;V*). If a < b, then the included trajectories have compact closure in L²(a,b;H).

The pivot-space bound needed for the temporal Arzelà–Ascoli argument is not an extra hypothesis: it follows quantitatively from the Lions–Magenes energy identity and the two stated L² bounds.

Quantitative Hilbert-valued one-dimensional H¹ estimate.

If u, du ∈ L²(a,b;H) and du is the weak time derivative of u, then the Lions–Magenes representative is continuous on [a,b] and satisfies

‖u(t)‖ ≤ sqrt (‖u‖² / (b-a) + 2 ‖u‖ ‖du‖)

at every time in the closed interval. It agrees almost everywhere with the original Bochner trajectory, so the same explicit estimate holds almost everywhere for that trajectory.

The constant is the standard non-sharp one-dimensional Sobolev estimate: choose an interior time where the squared norm equals its interval average, then apply the exact Hilbert-space energy identity and L² Hölder on the subinterval joining that time to t.

existsUnique_of_measurable_galerkin_garding_L2 constructs the unique Bochner class solving the integrated weak equation. This theorem adds the data that Evans uses to define the parabolic weak solution and its a priori theory:

  • the weak time derivative belongs to L²(a,b;V*);
  • u_t = ell - B(·)u almost everywhere;
  • the state has a representative continuous from [a,b] into the pivot Hilbert space H, with left trace equal to uInit;
  • the representative satisfies the Gårding energy estimate on every prefix [a,t].

Thus the measurable Galerkin construction produces a weak solution in the sense of Evans §7.1.1, with the continuity into H that Evans obtains from §5.9.2, Theorem 3.

PDE.Analysis.Evolution.HasWeakTimeDerivativeOn.{u_1} {X : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup X] [NormedSpace ℝ X] (U : Set ℝ) (f g : ℝ → X) : Prop

Local weak differentiation in time for functions valued in a real normed space. The definition records local Bochner integrability as well as the standard distributional identity against smooth scalar tests whose topological support lies in U. Including integrability is essential: Lean's Bochner integral is defined to be zero for a nonintegrable function, so the identity alone would not characterize a distributional derivative.

On Set.univ, this is the global weak-time-derivative predicate. On a proper open interval, compactly supported tests vanish near both endpoints, so the relation places no condition on endpoint traces or values outside the interval.

Nothing in the definition is specific to time: it is the weak derivative of any function of one real variable, and the De Gregorio profile files apply it to the spatial variable of a stationary profile.

• unfold id unfolds all occurrences of definition id in the target.

The simp tactic uses lemmas and hypotheses to simplify the main goal target or non-dependent hypotheses. It has many variants:

  • simp simplifies the main goal target using lemmas tagged with the attribute [simp].
  • simp [h₁, h₂, ..., hₙ] simplifies the main goal target using the lemmas tagged with the attribute [simp] and the given hᵢ's, where the hᵢ's are expressions.-
  • If an hᵢ is a defined constant f, then f is unfolded. If f has equational lemmas associated with it (and is not a projection or a reducible definition), these are used to rewrite with f.
  • simp [*] simplifies the main goal target using the lemmas tagged with the attribute [simp] and all hypotheses.
  • simp only [h₁, h₂, ..., hₙ] is like simp [h₁, h₂, ..., hₙ] but does not use [simp] lemmas.
  • simp [-id₁, ..., -idₙ] simplifies the main goal target using the lemmas tagged with the attribute [simp], but removes the ones named idᵢ.
  • simp at h₁ h₂ ... hₙ simplifies the hypotheses h₁ : T₁ ... hₙ : Tₙ. If the target or another hypothesis depends on hᵢ, a new simplified hypothesis hᵢ is introduced, but the old one remains in the local context.
  • simp at * simplifies all the hypotheses and the target.
  • simp [*] at * simplifies target and all (propositional) hypotheses using the other hypotheses.

positivity solves goals of the form 0 ≤ x, 0 < x and x ≠ 0. The tactic works recursively according to the syntax of the expression x, by attempting to prove subexpressions are positive/nonnegative/nonzero and combining this into a final proof. This tactic either closes the goal or fails.

For each subexpression e, positivity will try to:

  • try @[positivity]-tagged extensions to recursively prove e is positive/nonnegative/nonzero based on its subexpressions (see the positivity attribute for more details), or
  • try the norm_num tactic to prove e is positive/nonnegative/nonzero, or
  • try showing e : t is nonnegative because there is a CanonicallyOrderedAdd t instance, or
  • use a local hypothesis of the form 0 ≤ e, 0 < e or e ≠ 0.

This tactic is extensible. See the positivity attribute documentation for more details.

  • positivity [t₁, …, tₙ] first executes have := t₁; …; have := tₙ in the current goal, then runs positivity. This is useful when positivity needs derived premises such as 0 < y for division/reciprocal, or 0 ≤ x for real powers.

Examples:

example {a : ℤ} (ha : 3 < a) : 0 ≤ a ^ 3 + a := by positivity

example {a : ℤ} (ha : 1 < a) : 0 < |(3:ℤ) + a| := by positivity

example {b : ℤ} : 0 ≤ max (-3) (b ^ 2) := by positivity

example {a b c d : ℝ} (hab : 0 < a * b) (hb : 0 ≤ b) (hcd : c < d) :
    0 < a ^ c + 1 / (d - c) := by
  positivity [sub_pos_of_lt hcd, pos_of_mul_pos_left hab hb]

4204:
The have tactic is for adding opaque definitions and hypotheses to the local context of the main goal. The definitions forget their associated value and cannot be unfolded, unlike definitions added by the let tactic.

  • have h : t := e adds the hypothesis h : t if e is a term of type t.
  • have h := e uses the type of e for t.
  • have : t := e and have := e use this for the name of the hypothesis.
  • have pat := e for a pattern pat is equivalent to match e with | pat => _, where _ stands for the tactics that follow this one. It is convenient for types that have only one applicable constructor. For example, given h : p ∧ q ∧ r, have ⟨h₁, h₂, h₃⟩ := h produces the hypotheses h₁ : p, h₂ : q, and h₃ : r.
  • The syntax have (eq := h) pat := e is equivalent to match h : e with | pat => _, which adds the equation h : e = pat to the local context.

The tactic supports all the same syntax variants and options as the have term.

Properties and relations

  • It is not possible to unfold a variable introduced using have, since the definition's value is forgotten. The let tactic introduces definitions that can be unfolded.
  • The have h : t := e is like doing let h : t := e; clear_value h.
  • The have tactic is preferred for propositions, and let is preferred for non-propositions.
  • Sometimes have is used for non-propositions to ensure that the variable is never unfolded, which may be important for performance reasons. Consider using the equivalent let +nondep to indicate the intent.

4193:
Makes names from other namespaces visible without writing the namespace prefix.

Names that are made available with open are visible within the current section or namespace block. This makes referring to (type) definitions and theorems easier, but note that it can also make [scoped instances], notations, and attributes from a different namespace available.

The open command can be used in a few different ways:

  • open Some.Namespace.Path1 Some.Namespace.Path2 makes all non-protected names in Some.Namespace.Path1 and Some.Namespace.Path2 available without the prefix, so that Some.Namespace.Path1.x and Some.Namespace.Path2.y can be referred to by writing only x and y.

  • open Some.Namespace.Path hiding def1 def2 opens all non-protected names in Some.Namespace.Path except def1 and def2.

  • open Some.Namespace.Path (def1 def2) only makes Some.Namespace.Path.def1 and Some.Namespace.Path.def2 available without the full prefix, so Some.Namespace.Path.def3 would be unaffected.

    This works even if def1 and def2 are protected.

  • open Some.Namespace.Path renaming def1 → def1', def2 → def2' same as open Some.Namespace.Path (def1 def2) but def1/def2's names are changed to def1'/def2'.

    This works even if def1 and def2 are protected.

  • open scoped Some.Namespace.Path1 Some.Namespace.Path2 only opens [scoped instances], notations, and attributes from Namespace1 and Namespace2; it does not make any other name available.

  • open <any of the open shapes above> in makes the names open-ed visible only in the next command or expression.

Examples

/-- SKI combinators https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SKI_combinator_calculus -/
namespace Combinator.Calculus
  def I (a : α) : α := a
  def K (a : α) : β → α := fun _ => a
  def S (x : α → β → γ) (y : α → β) (z : α) : γ := x z (y z)
end Combinator.Calculus

section
  -- open everything under `Combinator.Calculus`, *i.e.* `I`, `K` and `S`,
  -- until the section ends
  open Combinator.Calculus

  theorem SKx_eq_K : S K x = I := rfl
end

-- open everything under `Combinator.Calculus` only for the next command (the next `theorem`, here)
open Combinator.Calculus in
theorem SKx_eq_K' : S K x = I := rfl

section
  -- open only `S` and `K` under `Combinator.Calculus`
  open Combinator.Calculus (S K)

  theorem SKxy_eq_y : S K x y = y := rfl

  -- `I` is not in scope, we have to use its full path
  theorem SKxy_eq_Iy : S K x y = Combinator.Calculus.I y := rfl
end

section
  open Combinator.Calculus
    renaming
      I → identity,
      K → konstant

  #check identity
  #check konstant
end

section
  open Combinator.Calculus
    hiding S

  #check I
  #check K
end

section
  namespace Demo
    inductive MyType
    | val

    namespace N1
      scoped infix:68 " ≋ " => BEq.beq

      scoped instance : BEq MyType where
        beq _ _ := true

      def Alias := MyType
    end N1
  end Demo

  -- bring `≋` and the instance in scope, but not `Alias`
  open scoped Demo.N1

  #check Demo.MyType.val == Demo.MyType.val
  #check Demo.MyType.val ≋ Demo.MyType.val
  -- #check Alias -- unknown identifier 'Alias'
end

has an H²(Ω) representative when the principal coefficients are W^{1,∞} with global ambient C¹ representatives, the lower-order coefficients are L∞, and f ∈ L²(Ω). The lower-order terms are absorbed into the L² effective forcing using the given H¹₀ solution.

Evans §6.3.1, interior H² regularity for general weak solutions.

Let u ∈ H¹(Ω) solve a uniformly elliptic divergence-form equation weakly, without any boundary condition. Every compact subset K ⊆ Ω has an open neighborhood V ⊆ Ω on which u has an H²(V) representative.

The proof uses two nested cutoffs. The outer cutoff turns u into an H¹₀(Ω) solution with an L² commutator forcing. The inner cutoff lies where the outer cutoff equals one, so the zero-trace difference-quotient theorem produces an H² representative of the original field near K.

Subtype.{u} {α : Sort u} (p : α → Prop) : Sort (max 1 u)

All the elements of a type that satisfy a predicate.

Subtype p, usually written { x : α // p x } or { x // p x }, contains all elements x : α for which p x is true. Its constructor is a pair of the value and the proof that it satisfies the predicate. In run-time code, { x : α // p x } is represented identically to α.

There is a coercion from { x : α // p x } to α, so elements of a subtype may be used where the underlying type is expected.

Examples:

  • { n : Nat // n % 2 = 0 } is the type of even numbers.
  • { xs : Array String // xs.size = 5 } is the type of arrays with five Strings.
  • Given xs : List α, List { x : α // x ∈ xs } is the type of lists in which all elements are contained in xs.

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

  • The recommended spelling of { x // p x } in identifiers is subtype.

cas proves the goal by computer algebra whose steps the kernel checks: identities, ideal memberships, determinants, derivatives, integrals, the theorems of the #cas commands and inequalities on bounded real variables.

Theorem

cas closes the goal and proves no other statement. It closes goals of these shapes:

  • an equality, disequality or order relation of ordinary terms that Mathlib's field_simp, ring, norm_num, positivity, linarith and nlinarith prove, and a real equality that the checked symbolic normalizer proves, such as Real.sin x ^ 2 + Real.cos x ^ 2 = 1;
  • Ideal.span {f₁, …, fₘ} = Ideal.span {g₁, …, gₖ} and f ∈ Ideal.span {g₁, …, gₘ} in a commutative ring, with cofactors from a Gröbner basis that ring checks;
  • the Gröbner property ∀ p ∈ Ideal.span S, p ≠ 0 → ∃ g ∈ S, MonomialOrder.lex.leadingTerm g ∣ MonomialOrder.lex.leadingTerm p of a set literal S in MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ, by Buchberger's criterion from divisions of its S-polynomials that the kernel checks;
  • a goal with determinants Matrix.det A of matrix literals, which cas evaluates first;
  • deriv f x = e, HasDerivAt f e x, HasDerivWithinAt f e s x, DifferentiableAt ℝ f x, and iteratedDeriv n f x = e and iteratedDerivWithin n f s x = e of a literal order n, nested derivatives such as deriv (fun x ↦ deriv f x) x included, by checked derivative rules;
  • Differentiable, DifferentiableOn, ContDiffAt, ContDiffOn, ContDiff, ContinuousAt, ContinuousOn, Continuous, AnalyticAt and AnalyticOnNhd over ℝ, by checked derivative and smoothness theorems; continuity, differentiability on a set and analyticity are the smoothness theorem at the orders 0, 1 and ω;
  • (∫ x in a..b, f x) = v and improper integrals such as (∫ t in Set.Ioi 0, f t) = v, also with their convergence, IntegrableOn f (Set.Ioi 0) ∧ ∫ t in Set.Ioi 0, f t = v, by the checked integration planner, which applies an analytic theorem, one integration by parts or a checked primitive;
  • Set.EqOn f g s and ApproxOn f g s 0 between ordinary functions, pointwise, and these two and ResidualBound r s 0 over checked symbolic expressions;
  • the printed theorems of the #cas commands: algebra, matrix and number theory results, limits at a rational point and at atTop and atBot, polynomial sign conditions and counts of real roots;
  • an inequality on real variables bounded by rational literal hypotheses, by the box route of cega.

Conditions and limits

The routes run in the order that CAS.ExactTactic.routeOrder lists: determinants, ideals, the theorems of the #cas commands, derivatives, integrals, the checked evaluator, the arithmetic script, equation hints and polynomial consequences of equation hypotheses, the checked identity route, the box route, the elementary rewrites (multiple-angle formulas, the exponential of a multiple of a logarithm and sums of real exponents, under the hypotheses they need), norm_num on a proposition without variables, and grind last, under the budget cas.grindHeartbeats. Other modules add routes with @[cas_route], and derivative backends for the Euclidean operators with @[cas_derivative_backend]. Every route checks its proof against the original goal. A derivative or an integral whose function needs a domain condition, such as x ≠ 0 for Real.log x, takes the evidence from cas using h; a nested derivative needs it only at the point. When every route fails, the goal is unchanged and the message lists what each route tried; the failure does not show that the goal is false.

Options

  • set_option cas.grindHeartbeats n sets the budget, in thousands of heartbeats, of the grind and norm_num fallbacks, default 20000; 0 turns them off.
  • set_option cas.maxDerivativeSteps n caps the goals of a proof by the derivative rules, default 512.
  • set_option trace.cas.fallback true shows the diagnostics of the grind fallback.
  • The forms cas using h, cas using [h₁, h₂], cas [l₁, l₂] and cas [integrate primitive := F], each documented in its own entry, pass domain evidence, local facts, simp lemmas and a primitive to the routes.

Examples

example (x : ℝ) : Real.sin x ^ 2 + Real.cos x ^ 2 = 1 := by
  cas

example (x : ℝ) (hx : x ≠ 0) : deriv (fun t : ℝ ↦ t * Real.log t) x = Real.log x + 1 := by
  cas using hx

example : (∫ x in (0 : ℝ)..1, x * Real.exp x) = 1 := by
  cas

example : AnalyticAt ℝ (fun x ↦ Real.exp (Real.sin x) / (1 + x ^ 2)) 0 := by
  cas

open Filter Topology in
example : Tendsto (fun x : ℝ ↦ (x ^ 2 + 1) / (2 * x ^ 2 - 3)) atTop (𝓝 (1 / 2)) := by
  cas

In a proof

theorem exp_lt_four (x : ℝ) (h₀ : 0 ≤ x) (h₁ : x ≤ 1) : Real.exp x < 4 := by
  have h : Real.exp x ≤ 3 := by cas
  linarith

The box route proves the bound from the hypotheses on x, and linarith uses it.

See also

Mathematica FullSimplify and Reduce, SymPy simplify. The tactics cas?, which suggests the call to keep in a proof, cas_nf and cega, and the #cas modes, whose printed theorems cas proves.

Possible issues

example (x : ℝ) : Real.sin x ^ 2 + Real.cos x ^ 2 = 2 := by
  cas

cas could not prove this arithmetic relation. The statement may be false, or it may lie outside
the supported normalization and arithmetic fragment

Here the statement is false. The rest of the message lists what each route tried, such as the difference -1 of the two sides that the checked normalizer computed.

example (x : ℝ) : deriv (fun x ↦ x ^ 2) x = 3 * x := by
  cas

cas computed a checked derivative, but it does not match the stated result.

#cas [derive x] (x ^ 2) prints the derivative that the route computed.

example (x : ℝ) : Real.exp x ≥ x + 1 := by
  cas

Box enclosure route:
  cas box route: no rational bounds on `x` in the hypotheses

Hypotheses a ≤ x and x ≤ b with rational literals give the box route a box. For every real x, Mathlib's Real.add_one_le_exp x proves this goal.

Extensions:

  • cas using h proves the goal with the side evidence h. On a semantic target h discharges the side conditions the route emits; on a derivative or integral goal it is the analytic domain evidence (a nonzero, positivity or branch hypothesis, or a Verified.Expr.ValidAt proof on the reflected route). Independently elaborated propositions are noted as local facts for the arithmetic and domain solvers, including applied proofs such as h 0. On an ordinary arithmetic goal the hint also enters the simp set and is evidence for the conditions recorded by the checked identity route. Juxtaposed complete proof hints are conjoined when they cannot elaborate as a single application; parentheses force a single term.

  • cas using [h₁, h₂] proves the goal with a list of complete proposition proofs as local facts. Inequalities and other propositions support arithmetic and domain discharge; only matching equalities are passed as hints to polynomial consequence search. The list contains proof terms, not simp directives, and incomplete evidence is rejected even when redundant.

  • cas [l₁, l₂] proves the goal with the listed local simp lemmas, which the reflected symbolic route and the arithmetic script of ordinary goals use. The arithmetic script also runs on a reflected equality that the reflected route does not prove, so lemmas such as Verified.Expr.eval can unfold its evaluations there. Before any route runs, the lemmas are elaborated as simp only [l₁, l₂] elaborates them, so an unknown name fails at once.

  • cas [integrate primitive := F] checks the supplied primitive F against the original integrand and applies the interval fundamental theorem of calculus. With using h, as in cas [integrate primitive := F using h], it checks F with the pointwise domain evidence h on the whole integration interval.

2892:
ENNReal.HolderTriple (p q : ENNReal) (r : semiOutParam ENNReal) : Prop

A class stating that p q r : ℝ≥0∞ satisfy p⁻¹ + q⁻¹ = r⁻¹. This is exactly the condition for which Hölder's inequality is valid (see MeasureTheory.MemLp.smul).

When r := 1, one generally says that p q are Hölder conjugate.

This class exists so that we can define a heterogeneous scalar multiplication on MeasureTheory.Lp, and this is why r must be marked as a semiOutParam. We don't mark it as an outParam because this would prevent Lean from using HolderTriple p q r and HolderTriple p q r' within a single proof, as may be occasionally convenient.

If you are defining a matrix, in terms of its entries, use of (fun i j ↦ _). The purpose of this approach is to ensure that terms of the form (fun i j ↦ _) * (fun i j ↦ _) do not appear, as the type of * can be misleading.

CAS.Verified.Expr.ValidAt.{u_1} {ι : Type u_1} (ρ : ι → ℝ) : CAS.Verified.Expr ι → Prop

Side conditions needed to justify the classical analytic derivative rules.

Rational literals carry a natural-number denominator in the AST, so validity rules out den = 0 there just as it rules out zero denominators for expression-level division.

For log, validity excludes zero, matching Mathlib's derivative theorem for the total real logarithm on both connected components of ℝ \ {0}. For sqrt, validity requires a strictly positive argument. This is stronger than what Mathlib's Real.hasDerivAt_sqrt needs (x ≠ 0, since Real.sqrt is constant on (-∞, 0]): it certifies the classical square-root branch rather than the totalized function, so a goal that is Lean-true only because of the extension to negative arguments is rejected by the reflective route. Lean's total Real.log/Real.sqrt have values outside those analytic domains, but these symbolic derivative rules certify classical differentiability. Raw Expr.eval itself is total and does not require ValidAt.

For rpow a b, validity requires a strictly positive base 0 < a, the hypothesis of Mathlib's HasFDerivAt.rpow; Lean's total Real.rpow has values for nonpositive bases that the classical power rule does not certify.

For asin and acos, validity excludes the two endpoints -1 and 1, matching Mathlib's derivative theorems for the total real inverse trigonometric functions. Arguments outside [-1, 1] are allowed: there the functions are locally constant and their derivatives are zero. Unlike sqrt and rpow, these cases do not restrict evaluation to the classical branch.

The universal set on a type α is the set containing all elements of α.

ContDiffOn.{u, uE, uF} (𝕜 : Type u) [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {E : Type uE} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type uF} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] (n : WithTop ℕ∞) (f : E → F) (s : Set E) : Prop

A function is continuously differentiable up to n on s if, for any point x in s, it admits continuous derivatives up to order n on a neighborhood of x in s. The parameter n belongs to ℕ∞ω (accessible in the ContDiff scope), i.e. it can be a natural number, ∞, or ω.

For n = ∞, we only require that this holds up to any finite order (where the neighborhood may depend on the finite order we consider). For n = ω, we require the function to be analytic within s at every point of s. The precise definition we give (all the derivatives should be analytic) is more involved to work around issues when the space is not complete, but it is equivalent when the space is complete.

Rellich compactness for H¹(Ω) → L²(Ω) under the operational Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas hypothesis. The order-zero inclusion

H¹(Ω) → L²(Ω)

is compact when Ω carries the operational chart-and-cutoff data used by the extension theorem. Deriving this hypothesis from the standard assertion that Ω has C¹ boundary is a separate geometric step.

The proof factors the inclusion in four steps. Extension.C1.extensionCLM sends H¹(Ω) boundedly into H¹(ℝ^n) and agrees with the original base function almost everywhere on Ω. Multiplying by a smooth compactly supported cutoff equal to one on closure Ω and restricting to a ball B containing its support lands continuously in H¹₀(B). The bounded-domain Rellich theorem for H¹₀(B) makes zero extension followed by the base-coordinate map compact, and precomposition keeps it compact. Finally restriction L²(ℝ^n) → L²(Ω) is bounded, and since the cutoff is one on Ω the composite is the order-zero inclusion.

If and only if, or logical bi-implication. a ↔ b means that a implies b and vice versa. By propext, this implies that a and b are equal and hence any expression involving a is equivalent to the corresponding expression with b instead.

For 1 ≤ n < p < ∞, every C¹ real-valued function on ℝ^n satisfies

|u(y)-u(x)| ≤ C(n,p) ‖Du‖ₚ |y-x|^(1-n/p).

No geometric potential hypothesis remains. The proof combines enorm_sub_ballAverage_le_morreyPotential, Hölder's inequality, and the exact polar integral of the Morrey kernel. The explicit constant below includes the enlargement factors 2^n and 2^(1-n/p).

Multidimensional finite-exponent Morrey estimate (Evans, PDE, §5.6.2, Theorem 4).

Let 1 ≤ n < p < ∞ and let q be conjugate to p. If the same-ball point-to-average estimate and the kernel estimate hold with constants A and K, then every pair of points satisfies

|u(y)-u(x)| ≤ 2 A K ‖Du‖_{Lᵖ(ℝ^n)} |y-x|^(1-n/p).

The proof compares both points to the average on the same n-dimensional ball and applies Hölder's inequality to the Riesz kernels. The unconditional enlarged-ball theorem below has no geometric assumptions and an explicit dimension-dependent factor in its constant.

MetricSpace.{u} (α : Type u) : Type u

A metric space is a type endowed with a ℝ-valued distance dist satisfying dist x y = 0 ↔ x = y, commutativity dist x y = dist y x, and the triangle inequality dist x z ≤ dist x y + dist y z.

See pseudometric spaces (PseudoMetricSpace) for the similar class with the dist x y = 0 ↔ x = y assumption weakened to dist x x = 0.

Any metric space is a T1 topological space and a uniform space (see TopologicalSpace, T1Space, UniformSpace), where the topology and uniformity come from the metric.

We make the uniformity/topology part of the data instead of deriving it from the metric. This e.g. ensures that we do not get a diamond when doing [MetricSpace α] [MetricSpace β] : TopologicalSpace (α × β): The product metric and product topology agree, but not definitionally so. See Note [forgetful inheritance].

A module is a generalization of vector spaces to a scalar semiring. a / b computes the result of dividing a by b. The meaning of this notation is type-dependent.

  • For most types like Nat, Int, Rat, Real, a / 0 is defined to be 0.
  • For Nat, a / b rounds downwards.
  • For Int, a / b rounds downwards if b is positive or upwards if b is negative. It is implemented as Int.ediv, the unique function satisfying a % b + b * (a / b) = a and 0 ≤ a % b < natAbs b for b ≠ 0. Other rounding conventions are available using the functions Int.fdiv (floor rounding) and Int.tdiv (truncation rounding).
  • For Float, a / 0 follows the IEEE 754 semantics for division, usually resulting in inf or nan.

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

  • The recommended spelling of / in identifiers is div.

Noncompact interpolation for all mixed derivatives of middle order n + 1.

The pure-axial row uses axial integration by parts; every positive-radial row uses radial integration by parts with its order-n predecessor. The successor identities identify both derivatives without commuting mixed partials. Local C² regularity is required only along these predecessor slices in r > 0, and the middle weight is differentiable there.

Weighted L² membership supplies the three square integrabilities and weighted measurabilities. The cross-term integrabilities and the two endpoint limits of each boundary product remain explicit. Neither compact support, a zero value trace on the axis, nor any row inequality is assumed.

Weight comparisons hold almost everywhere for the open-half-plane product measure. Zero extension supplies globally nonnegative weights to the Cauchy estimate without imposing conditions at the singular origin. The conclusion is one adjacent-order interpolation step.

The hypotheses: the all-axial order-n row is C² and compactly supported in z, every order-n row is C² and compactly supported in r, Φmid is C¹ in r and in z, the weights are nonnegative and satisfy hcompare0, hcompare1_axial and hcompare1_radial, and the weighted squares and cross terms are integrable and the weighted rows measurable on the half plane. No row inequality is assumed.

The hypothesis hradial_axis requires every order-n row, including the pure-axial row ∂_z^n f, to vanish on the axis r = 0. This restricts the theorem to data all of whose order-n rows have zero axis trace: at n = 0 to functions vanishing on the axis, as odd profiles do, and for n ≥ 1 it excludes even profiles whose even-exponent rows need not vanish there.

SobolevSpace.Weighted.HasLocallyComparableExhaustion {n k : ℕ} (w : SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.DerivIndex n k → ℝ^n → ENNReal) : Prop

For every realizable weighted graph U and accuracy ε there are: a graph V within ε/3 of U in the w-norm, a bounded reference weight v with a dominated weight q, and a sequence of test functions converging to V in the v-norm whose w-distance to V is eventually at most the q-distance plus ε/3 (EventuallyDistLeWeightedDistAdd).

All witnesses, including the comparison constants B and C, are chosen per U and ε. Since q = v = 0 and V = U are admissible, the predicate is equivalent to approximation of every realizable weighted graph by eligible test functions in the w-norm, arranged in the shape of the localize-compare-mollify argument.

if c then t else e is notation for ite c t e, "if-then-else", which decides to return t or e depending on whether c is true or false. Write if h : c then t else e instead for a "dependent if-then-else" dite, which allows t/e to use the fact that c is true/false.

13:
Eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → Prop

The equality relation. It has one introduction rule, Eq.refl. We use a = b as notation for Eq a b. A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.

variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd

Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value. That is, given h1 : a = b and h2 : p a, we can construct a proof for p b using substitution: Eq.subst h1 h2. Example:

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2

The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of Eq.subst and Eq.symm, and you can enter it by typing \t. For more information: Equality

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

  • The recommended spelling of = in identifiers is eq.

We use Mathlib's test-function type 𝓓((⊤ : Opens (ℝ^n)), ℝ) and require its tsupport (closed support) to lie in Ω. When Ω is open, this is the test class C_c^∞(Ω) of Evans §5.2.1.

Both f and its proposed weak derivative g are required to lie in L¹_loc(Ω), and the sign is (-1)^|α|, exactly as in Evans §5.2.1, (3). For an arbitrary set the predicate is still a well-formed test-function relation, but it is not automatically the standard Sobolev weak derivative: the test class can be too small (and can be trivial when Ω has empty interior), so uniqueness may fail. Results identifying this relation with the usual weak derivative therefore require openness or another explicit test-function density hypothesis.

List α is isomorphic to Array α, but they are useful for different things:

  • List α is easier for reasoning, and Array α is modeled as a wrapper around List α.
  • List α works well as a persistent data structure, when many copies of the tail are shared. When the value is not shared, Array α will have better performance because it can do destructive updates.

The L^q estimate for the singular kernel on a ball that is used in Evans §5.6.2.

SobolevSpace.HasBallAveragePotentialBound {n : ℕ} (u : ℝ^n → ℝ) (A : ENNReal) : Prop

The same-ball point-to-average potential estimate.

For a point x in the closed ball B̄(c,R), the oscillation from the ball average is controlled by the Riesz potential of |Du| over B(c,R). This is the multidimensional segment-averaging theorem in the proof of Evans §5.6.2, Theorem 4.

enorm_sub_ballAverage_le_morreyPotential proves the enlarged-ball form needed for Morrey's inequality. The predicate records the same-ball estimate used by the conditional theorems; the main theorem does not assume it, and the predicate alone does not encode Hölder continuity.
